thread.document:
I’d been struggling to reason about how information flows through attention and transformer blocks at a low level—specifically how the matrix multiplications and changing dimensions still produce an output with the same dimensionality as the input. I was also unclear on how multi-head attention differs from single-head attention and how the whole mechanism fits together.

To sort it out, I used Claude to build a visualization that traces the full path through a transformer. I iterated on it: starting with high-level questions, refining answers, and ending with a 14-step walkthrough that explains attention, the transformer block, and the computations between them.

Here is the published link of the visualization: https://claude.ai/public/artifacts/2ef271c0-bffd-4709-a7e4-cdc2d66bb2b8



As I went, my questions became more targeted, drilling into different parts of the architecture.

At the end, in addition to reviewing Claude's output, looking for any hallucinations, I also pasted the entire source code into GPT-5 to see if it could find any mistakes. GPT was able to point out some assumptions that Claude made that weren't as clear as they could have been. I took GPT's feedback and gave it to Claude for the final iteration of the tool.

Here is my annotated transcript:

comments.content: <document version="2.0"><paragraph>Interesting... It is interesting that it chose to do this using two essentially obsolete approaches --- learned additive position embeddings (basically entirely superseded by others at this point) and add-and-norm (this is a bit trickier --- nobody now would suggest this as the default because it is harder to get training to work reliably as compared to pre-norming and avoiding norms in the gradient path via skips... But it is still a bit controversial whether the pre-norm approach gives up a small bit of performance for unknown reasons, and when one is trying to train in very low precision things get trickier because dynamic range is at a premium.).<break/><break/>This represents an interesting drag on students' ability to learn --- we try in lecture, etc. to bring you all to the current state of best understanding and practice, but the LLMs with both older training cutoffs as well as the weight of the past sitting in their training data will pull you into the past.</paragraph><paragraph>It would be nice to see how students should properly push back against this when they themselves don't understand yet. </paragraph></document>
comments.document:
Interesting... It is interesting that it chose to do this using two essentially obsolete approaches --- learned additive position embeddings (basically entirely superseded by others at this point) and add-and-norm (this is a bit trickier --- nobody now would suggest this as the default because it is harder to get training to work reliably as compared to pre-norming and avoiding norms in the gradient path via skips... But it is still a bit controversial whether the pre-norm approach gives up a small bit of performance for unknown reasons, and when one is trying to train in very low precision things get trickier because dynamic range is at a premium.).

This represents an interesting drag on students' ability to learn --- we try in lecture, etc. to bring you all to the current state of best understanding and practice, but the LLMs with both older training cutoffs as well as the weight of the past sitting in their training data will pull you into the past.

It would be nice to see how students should properly push back against this when they themselves don't understand yet.

comments.content: <document version="2.0"><paragraph>The use of GPT nicely brought out the pre-norm thing. But was a bit overly polite about it. </paragraph><paragraph>It didn't call out the modern way of doing Feedforward (what MLPs are doing) using either Relu-squared or gated approaches. Instead, it went with the older GELU suggestion. </paragraph><paragraph/></document>

The use of GPT nicely brought out the pre-norm thing. But was a bit overly polite about it. 

It didn't call out the modern way of doing Feedforward (what MLPs are doing) using either Relu-squared or gated approaches. Instead, it went with the older GELU suggestion.
